content: The document provides detailed guidance on the medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, as established by the World Health Organization (WHO). It outlines the safety and appropriateness of various contraceptive methods for individuals with specific medical conditions or characteristics. The recommendations are based on the latest clinical and epidemiological evidence and are intended to assist policymakers, family planning program managers, and healthcare providers in delivering high-quality contraceptive services. Key Points: 1. Contraceptive Methods Covered: The document includes guidance on a wide range of contraceptive methods, such as combined oral contraceptives (COCs), combined patches, vaginal rings, injectable contraceptives, progestogen-only pills (POPs), implants, emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), copper intrauterine devices (Cu-IUDs), levonorgestrel-releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs), barrier methods, fertility awareness-based methods, lactational amenorrhea method (LAM), coitus interruptus, and male and female sterilization. 2. Medical Eligibility Categories: Each contraceptive method is classified into one of four categories based on its safety for individuals with specific medical conditions: Category 1: No restrictions for use. Category 2: Benefits generally outweigh theoretical or proven risks. Category 3: Risks usually outweigh benefits. Category 4: Unacceptable health risks if the method is used. 3. Special Considerations: Women over 40 years of age can generally use combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) (Category 2). Breastfeeding women less than six weeks postpartum should not use CHCs (Category 4), while those six weeks to six months postpartum are generally advised against CHC use (Category 3). After six months postpartum, CHCs are generally safe (Category 2). Postpartum women without other risk factors for venous thromboembolism (VTE) should avoid CHCs within 21 days postpartum (Category 3). After 42 days postpartum, CHCs can be used without restriction (Category 1). Women with superficial venous disorders, such as varicose veins, can use CHCs without restriction (Category 1). Those with superficial venous thrombosis (SVT) can generally use CHCs (Category 2). 4. Progestogen-Only Contraceptives (POCs): Breastfeeding women less than six weeks postpartum can generally use progestogen-only pills (POPs) and implants (Category 2) but are advised against progestogen-only injectables (Category 3). After six weeks postpartum, all POCs can be used without restriction (Category 1). 5. Levonorgestrel-Releasing IUDs (LNG-IUDs): Breastfeeding women less than 48 hours postpartum can generally use LNG-IUDs (Category 2). However, insertion between 48 hours and four weeks postpartum is generally not recommended (Category 3). After four weeks postpartum, LNG-IUDs can be used without restriction (Category 1). Women with puerperal sepsis should not have an LNG-IUD inserted (Category 4). 6. Emergency Contraceptive Pills (ECPs): ECPs are not applicable for pregnant women. Breastfeeding women can use combined oral contraceptives (COCs) or levonorgestrel (LNG) for emergency contraception without restriction (Category 1). Ulipristal acetate (UPA) is generally safe for breastfeeding women (Category 2). Women with a history of ectopic pregnancy, severe cardiovascular disease, or migraines can generally use COCs, LNG, or UPA for emergency contraception (Category 2). 7. Guideline Development: The fifth edition of the Medical Eligibility Criteria (MEC) was developed through consultations with experts and stakeholders, incorporating evidence from systematic reviews. The recommendations were formulated using the GRADE methodology, which assesses the quality of evidence and balances the benefits and risks of contraceptive use. 8. Target Audience: The guidance is intended for national family planning and reproductive health programs to develop localized guidelines. It is not a direct clinical guideline but serves as a reference for adapting recommendations to diverse healthcare settings. 9. Updates and Monitoring: WHO will review the recommendations every four years or sooner if new evidence emerges. Interim updates will be made available on WHO’s sexual and reproductive health web pages. 10. Encouragement for Research: WHO encourages further research to address unresolved issues related to contraceptive eligibility and invites feedback to improve the guidance. This document emphasizes the importance of balancing the safety of contraceptive methods with the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies, while considering individual medical conditions and circumstances.
